section: 1 · feature scaling: the inputs, once
text: A model that measures distance (k-nearest neighbours, SVMs with an RBF kernel, k-means), projects variance (PCA) or penalises weights uniformly (ridge, lasso) treats a unit of every feature the same, so a feature measured in thousands silently outvotes one measured in fractions.

section: 2 · one recipe, five choices of axes
text: 2 · One recipe, five choices of axes Every normalisation layer does the same three things to a tensor of activations: pick a set of numbers, compute their mean μ and variance σ², and replace each number x in the set with y = γ · (x − μ) / √(σ² + ε) + β μ, σ² mean and (biased, divide-by-n) variance over the set; RMSNorm skips μ and uses the mean square, so y = γ · x / √(mean(x²) + ε) ε a small constant against division by zero (10 −5 by default in PyTorch; LLM configs use 10 −5 or 10 −6 ) γ, β learned per feature or channel, initialised to 1 and 0, so the layer can undo the normalisation if that helps; without them, normalising would also limit what a layer can represent ( Ioffe and Szegedy 2015, §3 ) The kinds differ only in which numbers share one μ and σ , and that choice decides everything else: whether an example's output depends on the other examples in its batch, whether training and inference compute the same thing, and what the layer can be used for.
label: core
key: which numbers share one μ and σ

text: 4 · LayerNorm and RMSNorm: the same idea on the other axis LayerNorm normalises across the feature dimension, per data point, so every example (every token, in a transformer) is normalised independently, with one γ, β vector per layer ( Ba, Kiros and Hinton 2016 ).

section: 4 · layernorm and rmsnorm: the same idea on the other axis
text: It fixes all three BatchNorm weaknesses at once: it does not depend on batch size, it works for RNNs and transformers with variable-length inputs, and it computes the same thing at training and inference, with no running averages.

section: 7 · initialisation: choosing the scale of the first step
text: 7 · Initialisation: choosing the scale of the first step Scheme Idea Failure mode, or fit Constant (naive) the same value everywhere the symmetry problem : every neuron in a layer gets the same input and the same gradient, so they stay copies of each other and the network cannot diversify (the parent's Training lab preset "All-zero init never breaks symmetry") Plain random sample from some distribution breaks symmetry, but the scale is critical: variance too small and signals shrink layer by layer (vanishing gradients), too large and activations grow exponentially (exploding gradients) Xavier (Glorot) scale the variance by fan-in and fan-out, Var = 2/(n in + n out ); uniform and normal flavours sigmoid and tanh, whose activations are roughly linear and zero-mean around 0 He (Kaiming) Xavier modified for ReLU: variance doubled to 2/n in , because ReLU zeroes half the activations (its output has a non-zero mean and half the second moment) the ReLU-family default LeCun Var = 1/n in pairs with SELU (self-normalising networks) All variance-scaling schemes share one goal: keep activation and gradient variance roughly constant across layers, preventing vanishing or exploding gradients from step one.
label: core
